methods.label: Compare the units and leading columns
methods.explanation:
The units column and the leftmost column both add \(A+B\). Comparing their carries is useful because both produce the digit \(D\).

In the units column, either \(A+B=D\) or \(A+B=D+10\). In the leftmost column, \(A+B\), together with any incoming carry, equals \(D\), since the result has no sixth digit. Thus \(A+B\le D\). Combining these observations forces
\[
A+B=D,
\]
with no carry from the units column and no carry into the leftmost column.

The tens column now adds \(C+D\) and produces the digit \(D\). Therefore \(C\) must be 0: any positive digit \(C\le9\) would change the units digit of \(C+D\). With \(C=0\) and \(A+B=D\), the hundreds and thousands columns also work without carries.

Since the digits are distinct, \(A\) and \(B\) are distinct nonzero digits. Their smallest possible sum is \(1+2=3\), while \(D\) is at most 9. Hence only \(D=3,4,\ldots,9\) can occur.

Every one of these values works: choose \(A=1\), \(B=D-1\), and \(C=0\). These four digits are distinct, and every column satisfies the addition. We are counting the possible values of \(D\), so this gives exactly \(\boxed{7}\) values, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
methods.levelReason: Decimal place value, carries, and bounded digit reasoning suffice; no advanced number theory is used.

methods.label: Expand by place value
methods.explanation:
Writing each five-digit number by place value lets us collect all occurrences of each letter. Here an overline denotes the number formed by the displayed digits:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\overline{ABBCB}&=10000A+1101B+10C,\\
\overline{BCADA}&=101A+10000B+1000C+10D,\\
\overline{DBDDD}&=10111D+1000B.
\end{aligned}
\]
Substituting these expressions into the addition and collecting terms gives
\[
10101(A+B)+1010C=10101D,
\]
or
\[
10101(D-A-B)=1010C.
\]
Because \(C\) is a digit,
\[
0\le1010C\le9090<10101.
\]
The left side is an integer multiple of 10101. The only such multiple in this range is 0, so \(C=0\) and \(D=A+B\).

Distinctness now makes \(A\) and \(B\) distinct positive digits. Consequently \(3\le D\le9\). Conversely, for each \(D\) in this range, choose \(A=1\), \(B=D-1\), and \(C=0\). The digits are distinct and satisfy the collected equation, which is equivalent to the original addition. Thus every listed value is attainable, and there are exactly \(\boxed{7}\) possible values of \(D\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
